# Habeas corpus and fair trial (`habeas_corpus_fair_trial`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/institutions.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Institutions, law & governance (`institutions`)
- Deps: helped by rule_of_law, written_law_code
- Core idea: Nobody may be held without being brought promptly before a judge who is told the charge and must release him if there is no lawful ground (habeas corpus). At trial the accuser must prove the case with witnesses and evidence heard in public; the accused may answer, call witnesses and is not forced to confess; neutral judges or a jury of ordinary people decide. Torture is excluded because pain produces whatever the questioner wants, not the truth. The convincing argument: every rule protects the innocent man the ruler's enemies might accuse, and a confession under torture names more innocents.
- Pitfalls:
  - Thinking Magna Carta created trial by jury or habeas corpus: both grew later; the Habeas Corpus Act is 1679
  - Assuming pre-modern courts were lawless: Roman, Islamic and Chinese law had detailed rules of evidence, burden of proof and review of death sentences
  - Attacking judicial torture head-on: Roman-canon procedure required a confession or two eyewitnesses for conviction, so abolishing torture means first allowing conviction on circumstantial evidence
  - Believing juries were always impartial judges of fact: early English juries were neighbours expected to know the case already
  - Forgetting the gaoler: the writ is useless unless a named officer is personally fined or punished for ignoring it
- History: mesopotamia: c. 1754 BC – Hammurabi §§1–5: an accuser who cannot prove a capital charge is put to death; judges who alter a sealed verdict are removed; greece: 5th–4th c. BC – Athenian jury courts of 201 to 501 or more citizens chosen by lot, voting by secret ballot, with equal timed speeches; rome: 2nd c. AD – the burden of proof lies on the one who asserts (Digest 22.3.2); Trajan: better that the guilty go unpunished than the innocent be condemned (Digest 48.19.5); india: c. 3rd c. BC–3rd c. AD – Arthashastra and dharma texts set rules for witnesses, documents and judges, and limits on torture; china: 653 – Tang Code regulates interrogation, penalises false accusation and requires repeated review of death sentences by the throne; conviction still normally needs a confession; islamic: 7th–9th c. – proof lies on the claimant and the oath on the denier; fixed penalties are to be averted in case of doubt; no jury; europe: 1166 – Assize of Clarendon, juries of presentment; 1215 Magna Carta cl. 39; 1679 Habeas Corpus Act; 1764 Beccaria against torture and secret accusation; torture abolished in Prussia 1740–1754, Austria 1776, France 1780–1788; americas: 1791 – US Bill of Rights, Amendments 4–8
- Read:
  - Cesare Beccaria, Dei delitti e delle pene (1764)
  - John H. Langbein, Torture and the Law of Proof (1977)
  - Paul D. Halliday, Habeas Corpus: From England to Empire (2010)
